original: Everyone, please think of your biggest personal goal. For real -- you can take a second. You've got to feel this to learn it. Take a few seconds and think of your personal biggest goal, okay? Imagine deciding right now that you're going to do it. Imagine telling someone that you meet today what you're going to do. Imagine their congratulations, and their high image of you. Doesn't it feel good to say it out loud? Don't you feel one step closer already, like it's already becoming part of your identity? Well, bad news: you should have kept your mouth shut, because that good feeling now will make you less likely to do it. The repeated psychology tests have proven that telling someone your goal makes it less likely to happen. Any time you have a goal, there are some steps that need to be done, some work that needs to be done in order to achieve it. Ideally you would not be satisfied until you'd actually done the work. But when you tell someone your goal and they acknowledge it, psychologists have found that it's called a "social reality." The mind is kind of tricked into feeling that it's already done. And then because you've felt that satisfaction, you're less motivated to do the actual hard work necessary. So this goes against conventional wisdom that we should tell our friends our goals, right? So they hold us to it. So, let's look at the proof. 1926: Kurt Lewin, founder of social psychology, called this "substitution." 1933: Wera Mahler found when it was acknowledged by others, it felt real in the mind. 1982, Peter Gollwitzer wrote a whole book about this, and in 2009, he did some new tests that were published. It goes like this: 163 people across four separate tests. Everyone wrote down their personal goal. Then half of them announced their commitment to this goal to the room, and half didn't. Then everyone was given 45 minutes of work that would directly lead them towards their goal, but they were told that they could stop at any time. Now, those who kept their mouths shut worked the entire 45 minutes on average, and when asked afterward, said that they felt that they had a long way to go still to achieve their goal. But those who had announced it quit after only 33 minutes, on average, and when asked afterward, said that they felt much closer to achieving their goal. So if this is true, what can we do? Well, you could resist the temptation to announce your goal. You can delay the gratification that the social acknowledgment brings, and you can understand that your mind mistakes the talking for the doing. But if you do need to talk about something, you can state it in a way that gives you no satisfaction, such as, "I really want to run this marathon, so I need to train five times a week and kick my ass if I don't, okay?" So audience, next time you're tempted to tell someone your goal, what will you say? Exactly! Well done.

Now, imagine deciding right now that you will achieve it. Picture telling someone you meet today about your goal. Imagine them congratulating you and thinking highly of you. When you have a goal, you need to take some steps and do some work to achieve it. Ideally, you would not feel satisfied until you have done the work. But when you tell someone your goal and they recognize it, psychologists say this creates a "social reality." Your mind is tricked into feeling that the goal is already done. Because you feel that satisfaction, you become less motivated to do the hard work needed. This goes against the common idea that we should tell our friends our goals. We do this so they can help us stay on track. Let's look at the evidence. In 1926, Kurt Lewin, who started social psychology, called this "substitution." In 1933, Wera Mahler found that when others acknowledged our goals, they felt real in our minds. In 1982, Peter Gollwitzer wrote a whole book about this. In 2009, he did some new tests that were published. Here’s what happened: 163 people took part in four different tests. Everyone wrote down their personal goal. Half of the people in the room said they were committed to their goal, and half did not. Everyone then got 45 minutes of work that would help them reach their goal. They were told they could stop working at any time. The people who did not say anything worked for the full 45 minutes, on average. When they were asked later, they felt they still had a long way to go to reach their goal. But the people who announced their goal stopped working after only 33 minutes, on average. When they were asked later, they felt much closer to reaching their goal. So, if this is true, what can we do? You could try not to announce your goal. You can wait for the satisfaction that comes from others noticing your goal. You can realize that talking about your goal can feel like you are doing something. If you need to talk about your goal, you can say it in a way that does not make you feel good, like, "I really want to run this marathon, so I need to train five times a week and push myself if I don't, okay?"
